questions.stem: Marram grass grows on sand dunes and has leaves that can roll up. How does leaf rolling help the plant survive in its dry, windy environment?

options.text: Rolling up traps sunlight inside the leaf for more photosynthesis
Rolling traps a layer of humid air inside, reducing the water vapour concentration gradient and decreasing transpiration
Rolling prevents sand from entering the stomata
Rolling makes the leaves stronger against wind

questions.explanation: When marram grass leaves roll inward, the stomata (on the inner surface) become enclosed in a sheltered space. Humid air from transpiration becomes trapped inside, reducing the concentration gradient between the leaf interior and the air outside. This significantly reduces the rate of water loss by transpiration, critical for survival on exposed sand dunes.

questions.stem: Cacti have adapted to desert conditions by developing thick, fleshy stems and spines instead of leaves. How do these adaptations help reduce water loss?

options.text: Spines produce extra water through photosynthesis
Thick stems store water; spines (reduced leaves) have a much smaller surface area than flat leaves, greatly reducing transpiration
Spines absorb moisture from the air
Thick stems block sunlight from reaching the roots

questions.explanation: Cacti store water in their thick, fleshy stems (which also carry out photosynthesis). Leaves are reduced to spines, which have a tiny surface area compared to flat leaves, massively reducing the surface area from which water can be lost. Spines also provide shade and protection from herbivores. These are classic xerophyte adaptations.

questions.stem: Water lilies (hydrophytes) have stomata on the UPPER surface of their floating leaves, unlike most land plants. Why?

options.text: The upper surface receives more rain
The lower surface is in contact with water, so stomata there would be blocked; the upper surface is exposed to air for gas exchange
Upper stomata absorb more light for photosynthesis
It is a random evolutionary accident

questions.explanation: Water lily leaves float on the water surface. The lower surface is in direct contact with water, which would flood and block any stomata there. Having stomata on the upper surface (exposed to air) allows normal gas exchange -- CO2 can enter for photosynthesis and O2 can be released. This is the opposite arrangement to most land plants.

questions.stem: Hydrophytes often have large air spaces (aerenchyma) in their stems and leaves. What is the function of this tissue?

options.text: To store extra water for dry periods
To provide buoyancy so leaves float at the surface, and to allow gases (especially oxygen) to reach waterlogged roots
To strengthen the plant structure
To increase the rate of transpiration

questions.explanation: Aerenchyma (air-filled tissue) serves two key functions in hydrophytes: it provides buoyancy, helping leaves float at the water surface where they receive light for photosynthesis; and it creates internal channels for oxygen to diffuse from the leaves down to the submerged roots, which would otherwise be in oxygen-depleted waterlogged soil.

questions.stem: Some xerophytes have sunken stomata (stomata located in pits in the leaf surface). How does this adaptation reduce water loss?

options.text: Sunken stomata receive less light
The pits trap a pocket of humid air above the stomata, reducing the water vapour concentration gradient and slowing transpiration
Sunken stomata can close more tightly
Sunken stomata absorb water from the air

questions.explanation: Sunken stomata sit in small depressions or pits in the leaf surface. Water vapour escaping through the stomata accumulates in these pits, creating a pocket of humid air. This reduces the concentration gradient between the moist interior of the leaf and the drier external air, slowing the rate of diffusion of water vapour out of the leaf.
